auth.description: Supabase project anon (publishable) key. Travels as the `apikey` header on every request. Requests made with it run as the project's `anon` Postgres role, so everything they return is bounded by the project's row-level-security policies — it is not the `service_role` key and confers none of that key's authority
auth.name: supabase.anon_key
auth.subject: unstated

config.help: The reference id of your project, from Project Settings → General, or the first label of your project's URL. Paste only that label — not the full `https://…` URL and not anything with an `@` in it: the ref becomes the hostname every request goes to, so a value carrying an `@` would send this project's key to a host you did not name
config.label: Supabase project ref
config.name: project_ref

config.help: From Project Settings → API, copy the key labelled `anon` / `public` (newer projects spell it `sb_publishable_…`). Do NOT paste the `service_role` key, even though it also works: `service_role` bypasses row-level security completely, so a connector holding it can read and change every row in your database regardless of the policies you wrote. The anon key is the one Supabase publishes as safe to expose, and it is all this connector needs
config.label: Supabase anon (publishable) key
config.name: anon_key

description: Supabase project data and configuration: describe the tables the API exposes, read a table's rows, and read which sign-in methods the project has enabled. Reads only, through the project's public anon key, so every row returned is bounded by the project's own row-level-security policies

operations.description: Describe the tables, views and columns this project's data API exposes, as an OpenAPI 2.0 document. Takes no argument. Call this first to discover the table names supabase-rows-list takes and what columns each one has — the document reflects only what the anon role may see, so a table absent from it is a table this key cannot read. Also this connector's `verify`: a bounded read that runs unattended and needs nothing configured beyond the project ref and the key

basePath.description: The path prefix every documented path hangs off — `/`

definitions.description: One key per exposed table or view, each carrying that relation's `properties` — the column names, their types, and PostgREST's own notes. This is where a caller reads what a row looks like

host.description: The project's API host, as PostgREST sees it

info.description: Title, description and version of the exposed schema, as PostgREST reports them

parameters.description: PostgREST's shared query parameters — `select`, `order`, `limit`, `offset` and the filter operators. Note that this connector declares only `limit`; see the file header for the rest

paths.description: One key per exposed table, view and function, each `/<name>`. The key without its leading slash is what supabase-rows-list's `table` argument takes

swagger.description: The OpenAPI version of this document — `2.0`

operations.description: Read rows from one table or view in this project. Returns a JSON array of row objects with every column the anon role may read; the columns are the project's own, so call supabase-schema-describe first to learn them. Row-level security decides which rows come back — an empty array means the policies matched nothing, not that the table is empty. This connector cannot filter, project or sort: pass `limit` to bound the read and do the rest in the flow

params.description: The table or view to read, exactly as it appears under `paths` in supabase-schema-describe's response, without the leading slash. Must be a relation the project exposes to its API — a name the schema document does not list is not readable with this key
params.name: table

params.description: Maximum number of rows to return. Omitting it returns every row the policies match, up to the ceiling the project's own API settings impose (1000 by default) — pass a value rather than relying on that, because the ceiling is per-project and can be raised
params.name: limit

operations.description: Read which sign-in methods this project has enabled, and whether self-service sign-up is open. Takes no argument and returns configuration only — no user data and no identities. Use it to decide whether a flow can offer a given provider before it tries

disable_signup.description: True when self-service sign-up is off, so only an existing user can sign in

external.description: One boolean per external identity provider the project may enable — `google`, `github`, `apple`, `azure` and the rest — true where it is configured and turned on. Left untyped rather than enumerated: the key set follows whichever providers Supabase currently supports, and a fixed list here would be wrong on their next release

mailer_autoconfirm.description: True when a new email address is trusted without a confirmation link

phone_autoconfirm.description: True when a new phone number is trusted without an SMS code

saml_enabled.description: True when SAML single sign-on is available on this project

sms_provider.description: The configured SMS provider's name, or empty when there is none
